subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: Earth's mass is about 81 times the mass of the Moon. How does the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on the Moon by Earth compare with the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on Earth by the Moon?
options: The force on the Moon is 81 times as large.
The force on each has exactly the same magnitude.
The force on Earth is 81 times the force on the Moon.
The force on Earth is zero; the Moon is too small.
optionWhy: A student who believes the more massive body exerts the larger force picks this. In G m_1m_2/r² the two masses appear as a product, which is the same number for the force on the Moon and the force on Earth, so the forces have equal magnitudes.

Newton's law of universal gravitation gives the magnitude of both forces as G m_Earth m_Moon/r², with the same product of masses and the same distance r, so they are equal; they are the two forces of one interaction, a Newton's third-law pair. The Moon's motion changes far more only because the same size of force acts on a much smaller mass.

A student who thinks the force on a body depends only on that body's own mass, as F_g = mg seems to say, picks this. Both masses appear in G m_1m_2/r²: the Moon's small mass reduces its pull on Earth by exactly as much as Earth's large mass increases it, so the two forces are equal in magnitude.

A student who thinks a small body cannot pull on a much larger one picks this. Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass: the Moon pulls on Earth with a force equal in magnitude to Earth's pull on the Moon. Earth's motion changes only slightly because its mass is so large.
questions.explain: Newton's law of universal gravitation gives the magnitude of both forces as G m_Earth m_Moon/r², with the same product of masses and the same distance r, so they are equal; they are the two forces of one interaction, a Newton's third-law pair. The Moon's motion changes far more only because the same size of force acts on a much smaller mass.

questions.q: An astronaut floats at rest near her spacecraft, far from any planet or star. Which statement about gravitational forces between the astronaut and the spacecraft is correct?
options: Each pulls the other, but the craft pulls harder.
Neither pulls; gravity needs a planet or a star.
Each one pulls the other toward itself.
The craft pulls her, but she does not pull it.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the more massive object exerts the larger force picks this. The two pulls form a Newton's third-law pair: each has magnitude G m_astronaut m_craft/r², so they are equal in magnitude. The same force changes the astronaut's motion more only because her mass is smaller.

A student who thinks only astronomical bodies exert gravitational forces picks this. Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass; the force between an astronaut and a spacecraft is small because G is small, not because it is absent.

Gravitational forces are attractive and act between any two objects with mass, in space as anywhere else. The astronaut pulls the spacecraft toward her and the spacecraft pulls her toward it, with forces of equal magnitude. With everyday masses and distances the forces are tiny, because G is so small, but they are not zero.

A student who thinks a small object cannot pull on a larger one picks this. Gravitational attraction is mutual: the astronaut pulls on the spacecraft with a force of the same magnitude as the spacecraft's pull on her.
questions.explain: Gravitational forces are attractive and act between any two objects with mass, in space as anywhere else. The astronaut pulls the spacecraft toward her and the spacecraft pulls her toward it, with forces of equal magnitude. With everyday masses and distances the forces are tiny, because G is so small, but they are not zero.

questions.q: The diagram shows a space probe moving up and to the left along the dashed path, with Earth and the Moon also shown. Four arrows are drawn from the probe. Which arrow shows the direction of the gravitational force exerted on the probe by the Moon?
options: Arrow 1
Arrow 3
Arrow 4
Arrow 2
optionWhy: A student who thinks the force on a moving object points along its motion picks this. The gravitational force does not depend on the direction of the velocity; the force exerted by the Moon points along the line from the probe to the Moon's center.

A student who thinks every gravitational force points toward Earth picks this. Arrow 3 shows the direction of the force exerted on the probe by Earth. The force exerted by the Moon points toward the Moon's center.

A student who thinks gravity always points 'down' picks this. Down the page is not a special direction here: the Moon's gravitational force on the probe points toward the Moon's center, up and to the right.

The gravitational force is attractive and is exerted along the line joining the centers of mass of the two objects. The force exerted on the probe by the Moon therefore points from the probe directly toward the Moon's center, which is arrow 2.
questions.explain: The gravitational force is attractive and is exerted along the line joining the centers of mass of the two objects. The force exerted on the probe by the Moon therefore points from the probe directly toward the Moon's center, which is arrow 2.
questions.working: The gravitational force is attractive and is exerted along the line joining the centers of mass, so the Moon's force on the probe points from the probe toward the Moon's center: arrow 2. Arrow 3 is the direction of Earth's force on the probe; the probe's velocity (arrow 1) and 'down the page' (arrow 4) do not set the direction of either gravitational force.

questions.q: Point P is in empty space near Mars, and there is no object at P. Which statement about the gravitational field of Mars at point P is correct?
options: There is no field at P until an object is placed there to feel it.
The field at P would be stronger if a more massive object were placed there.
It has a value at P giving the force per kilogram on any object put there.
There is no field at P if P lies above the top of Mars's atmosphere.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a field exists only where an object detects it picks this. The field is created by Mars, and GM/r² contains only Mars's mass and the distance from its center; an object placed at P measures the field but does not create it.

A student who confuses field strength with force picks this. A more massive object at P would have a larger force exerted on it, but in proportion to its mass, so the force per kilogram, the field strength, is the same for any object.

A field models the effect of a noncontact force at every point in space. Mars's gravitational field exists at P whether or not anything is there; its value tells us the gravitational force per kilogram that any object placed at P would experience, and it is set by Mars's mass and the distance from Mars's center.

A student who thinks gravity needs air, or stops where space begins, picks this. Mars's field extends through empty space, getting weaker with distance from its center but never stopping at the top of the atmosphere.
questions.explain: A field models the effect of a noncontact force at every point in space. Mars's gravitational field exists at P whether or not anything is there; its value tells us the gravitational force per kilogram that any object placed at P would experience, and it is set by Mars's mass and the distance from Mars's center.

questions.q: A suitcase is set down at rest on a horizontal conveyor belt that moves at a constant speed. For a short time the suitcase slides on the belt; after that it moves along with the belt. Instant 1 is during the sliding, and instant 2 is after the suitcase moves along with the belt. Which statement correctly compares the kinetic friction force exerted on the suitcase at the two instants?
options: It is the same at both instants, as the suitcase is moving at both.
It acts forward at instants 1 and 2, as a force must keep it moving.
It is exerted at instant 1 only, while the suitcase slides on the belt.
It is zero at both instants, since friction cannot speed the suitcase up.
optionWhy: A student who thinks kinetic friction acts whenever an object moves relative to the ground picks this. What matters is motion relative to the belt: at instant 2 the suitcase moves with the belt, the surfaces do not slide, and there is no kinetic friction.

A student who believes a moving object needs a force in its direction of motion to keep it moving picks this. At instant 1 kinetic friction does point forward, but at instant 2 the suitcase moves at constant velocity with the belt: no force is needed to keep it moving, and because the surfaces do not slide there is no kinetic friction (nor any static friction).

Kinetic friction occurs only while two surfaces in contact move relative to each other. At instant 1 the belt moves faster than the suitcase, so the surfaces slide and kinetic friction acts, pointing forward and speeding the suitcase up. At instant 2 the suitcase and belt have the same velocity, so there is no kinetic friction.

A student who believes friction can only oppose an object's motion picks this, and decides the belt simply 'carries' the suitcase. While the suitcase slides, it moves backward relative to the belt, so kinetic friction on it points forward and is what speeds it up.
questions.explain: Kinetic friction occurs only while two surfaces in contact move relative to each other. At instant 1 the belt moves faster than the suitcase, so the surfaces slide and kinetic friction acts, pointing forward and speeding the suitcase up. At instant 2 the suitcase and belt have the same velocity, so there is no kinetic friction.
questions.working: Kinetic friction needs the two surfaces in contact to move relative to each other. Instant 1: the belt moves faster than the suitcase, so the suitcase slides backward relative to the belt and kinetic friction, magnitude μ_k F_N, acts on it in the belt's direction of motion, speeding it up. Instant 2: suitcase and belt have the same velocity, so there is no relative motion and no kinetic friction (and, with the belt at constant speed, no static friction either). So kinetic friction acts at instant 1 only.

questions.q: A rectangular wooden block, sanded smooth on every face, slides across a wooden table. Which change would alter the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface it slides on?
options: Placing a heavy load on top of the block as it slides
Turning the block onto a face with a smaller area
Sliding the block on a sheet of glass laid on the table
Pushing the block so that it slides at a much greater speed
optionWhy: A student who thinks the coefficient grows with the object's weight picks this. A load increases the normal force and so the friction force, but the ratio F_f/F_N, μ_k, stays the same because the surfaces are unchanged.
A student who thinks the area of contact affects friction picks this. Every face is the same sanded wood, and neither the friction force nor μ_k depends on the area of contact.
The coefficient of kinetic friction depends on the materials of the two surfaces in contact. Sliding on glass replaces a wood–wood pair with a wood–glass pair, which has a different μ_k.
A student who thinks kinetic friction grows with speed picks this. In the friction model used in AP Physics 1, μ_k depends only on the materials of the two surfaces, not on how fast they slide.
questions.explain: The coefficient of kinetic friction depends on the materials of the two surfaces in contact. Sliding on glass replaces a wood–wood pair with a wood–glass pair, which has a different μ_k.

questions.q: A block slides down a rough ramp. The diagram shows four arrows, labeled P, Q, R and S, drawn from the center of the block. Which arrow shows the direction of the normal force exerted on the block by the ramp?
options: Arrow P
Arrow R
Arrow Q
Arrow S
optionWhy: A student who thinks the normal force always points straight up picks this. That is true only on a level surface. On a ramp the normal force is perpendicular to the ramp's surface, tilted from the vertical by the ramp's angle.

The normal force is the component of the ramp's contact force perpendicular to the ramp's surface, and it is directed away from the surface. Arrow R is at right angles to the ramp and points away from it.

A student who thinks the normal force points into the surface picks this. Arrow Q is the direction of the force the block exerts on the ramp. The force exerted on the block by the ramp points the opposite way, away from the ramp.

A student who thinks the normal force is the block's weight pressing on the ramp picks this. Arrow S is the direction of the gravitational force exerted by Earth; the normal force is a different force, exerted by the ramp, perpendicular to its surface.
questions.explain: The normal force is the component of the ramp's contact force perpendicular to the ramp's surface, and it is directed away from the surface. Arrow R is at right angles to the ramp and points away from it.

questions.q: A suitcase stands on the floor of a train carriage while the train moves along a straight, level track. Which condition means that the suitcase is slipping (sliding) on the floor?
options: It is moving relative to the ground beside the track.
Its velocity differs from the velocity of the floor beneath it.
The train speeds up, and the suitcase tends to stay behind.
The floor exerts a friction force on the suitcase.
optionWhy: A student who thinks sliding means moving relative to the ground picks this. A suitcase carried along at the train's velocity moves past the ground but does not slip on the floor; slipping is motion relative to the surface it touches.
Slipping and sliding mean that the two surfaces in contact move relative to each other. The suitcase slips on the floor exactly when its velocity is not the same as the floor's.

A student who takes a tendency to slip for slipping picks this. While the train speeds up, static friction can speed the suitcase up with it; the suitcase slips only if the friction needed exceeds μ_s F_N.
A student who thinks friction acts only on sliding objects picks this. Static friction can act on the suitcase while it does not slip, for example while the train speeds up gently.
questions.explain: Slipping and sliding mean that the two surfaces in contact move relative to each other. The suitcase slips on the floor exactly when its velocity is not the same as the floor's.

questions.q: In a lab, a student models a spring as an ideal spring. Which statement describes how an ideal spring behaves?
options: Its force is proportional to its length, measured end to end.
Its force doubles when its stretch doubles; its mass is negligible.
Its force is the same however far it is stretched or compressed.
Its force depends on how fast the attached object is moving.
optionWhy: A student who thinks spring force depends on total length picks this. The force is proportional to the change in length from the relaxed length; at its relaxed length a spring exerts no force, however long it is.
An ideal spring has negligible mass and exerts a force proportional to its change in length from its relaxed length, so doubling the stretch doubles the force.
A student who treats a spring force as a fixed property of the spring picks this. The force of an ideal spring grows in proportion to its change in length and is zero at the relaxed length.
A student who links force with speed picks this. The force of an ideal spring depends only on its change in length at that instant, whatever the velocity of the object attached to it.
questions.explain: An ideal spring has negligible mass and exerts a force proportional to its change in length from its relaxed length, so doubling the stretch doubles the force.

questions.q: An ideal spring has a relaxed length of 10 cm. When it is stretched to a length of 14 cm, it exerts a force of magnitude 3.0 N on the object attached to it. What is the magnitude of the force it exerts when it is stretched to a length of 22 cm?
optionWhy: A student who takes the force to be proportional to the total length scales by 22/14 and gets 4.7 N. The force is proportional to the change in length from 10 cm, which triples.
A student who measures the change in length from 14 cm uses Δx = 8 cm and gets 6.0 N. The change in length is measured from the relaxed length: 22 cm − 10 cm = 12 cm.
A student who thinks a spring exerts the same force however far it is stretched keeps 3.0 N. An ideal spring's force is proportional to its change in length, which has tripled.
The change in length triples, from 4 cm to 12 cm (both measured from the 10 cm relaxed length), so the force triples: 3 × 3.0 N = 9.0 N.
questions.explain: The change in length triples, from 4 cm to 12 cm (both measured from the 10 cm relaxed length), so the force triples: 3 × 3.0 N = 9.0 N.
questions.working: Change in length from the relaxed length: Δx₁ = 14 cm − 10 cm = 4 cm and Δx₂ = 22 cm − 10 cm = 12 cm. The force is proportional to the change in length, so F₂ = (12 cm/4 cm)(3.0 N) = 3 × 3.0 N = 9.0 N.

questions.q: The graph shows the magnitude F of the force exerted by an ideal spring as a function of the spring's length L, from its relaxed length to a length of 20 cm. What is the spring constant of the spring?
options: 15 N/m
optionWhy: The spring constant is the slope of the line. The spring's relaxed length is 10 cm, so at 20 cm, Δx = 0.10 m and k = 1.5 N/0.10 m = 15 N/m.

A student who divides the force by the total length, 1.5 N/0.20 m, gets 7.5 N/m. The force is proportional to the change in length from 10 cm, not to the length, which is why the line does not pass through the origin.
A student who divides by the change in length in centimeters, 1.5 N/10 cm, gets 0.15. In SI units the change in length is 0.10 m, so k = 15 N/m.
A student who takes the area under the graph, ½(1.5 N)(0.10 m) = 0.075 N·m, as the spring constant picks this. The spring constant is the slope of the graph, 15 N/m.
questions.explain: The spring constant is the slope of the line. The spring's relaxed length is 10 cm, so at 20 cm, Δx = 0.10 m and k = 1.5 N/0.10 m = 15 N/m.
questions.working: The relaxed length is where F = 0: L = 10 cm. At L = 20 cm, Δx = 20 cm − 10 cm = 10 cm = 0.10 m and F = 1.5 N. k = F/Δx = 1.5 N/0.10 m = 15 N/m, which is the slope of the line.

questions.q: An object of mass 0.20 kg hangs at rest from a vertical ideal spring, which is stretched 5.0 cm from its relaxed length. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the spring constant of the spring?
options: 40 N/m
optionWhy: A student who uses the mass, 0.20 kg, in place of the weight gets 0.20/0.050 = 4.0. The spring force balances the weight, mg = 2.0 N, so k = 40 N/m.
A student who divides the weight by the stretch in centimeters, 2.0 N/5.0 cm, gets 0.40. The stretch must be in meters, 0.050 m, giving 40 N/m.
The object is at rest, so the spring force balances the gravitational force: kΔx = mg = 2.0 N. With Δx = 0.050 m, k = 2.0 N/0.050 m = 40 N/m.
A student who thinks k measures how easily a spring stretches divides the stretch by the force: 0.050 m/2.0 N = 0.025. The spring constant is force per unit stretch, k = F/Δx = 40 N/m.
questions.explain: The object is at rest, so the spring force balances the gravitational force: kΔx = mg = 2.0 N. With Δx = 0.050 m, k = 2.0 N/0.050 m = 40 N/m.
questions.working: At rest, the spring force balances the gravitational force: kΔx = mg = (0.20 kg)(10 m/s²) = 2.0 N. Δx = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m, so k = 2.0 N/0.050 m = 40 N/m.

questions.q: A pendulum bob is released from rest at point X. It swings through its lowest point to point Y on the other side, then swings back toward X, and the motion repeats. Which of the following is the period of the pendulum?
options: The time for the bob to swing out from X to Y and back to X
The time the bob takes to travel from X to Y for the first time
The number of full swings the bob makes each second
The total time the bob keeps swinging until it comes to rest
optionWhy: The period is the time for one full cycle of the motion. The cycle starts at X and is complete when the bob is back at X, ready to repeat the same motion: a swing out to Y and back.
A student who counts one swing as a cycle picks this. The swing from X to Y is only half the cycle; the motion does not start to repeat until the bob has swung back to X.
A student who confuses period with frequency picks this. The number of full swings (cycles) each second is the frequency, f; the period is the time for one cycle, T = 1/f.
A student who reads 'period' as a whole stretch of time picks this. The period is the time for ONE cycle; a pendulum that swings for a long time completes many periods.
questions.explain: The period is the time for one full cycle of the motion. The cycle starts at X and is complete when the bob is back at X, ready to repeat the same motion: a swing out to Y and back.

questions.q: A wheel turns at a constant rate with a frequency of 4.0 Hz. Which statement about the wheel's motion is correct?
options: It takes 4.0 s to complete each revolution.
A point on its rim moves at a speed of 4.0 m/s.
It completes 4.0 revolutions in each minute.
It completes 4.0 revolutions every second.
optionWhy: A student who confuses frequency with period picks this. The time for one revolution is the period, T = 1/f = 1/(4.0 Hz) = 0.25 s.
A student who reads the frequency as a speed picks this. The rim speed is 2πr multiplied by the frequency and depends on the wheel's radius, which is not given.
A student who takes hertz to mean revolutions per minute picks this. 1 Hz is one revolution per SECOND, so 4.0 Hz is 240 revolutions per minute.
Frequency is the number of revolutions completed per unit time, and 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹, one revolution per second. So 4.0 Hz means 4.0 revolutions each second, and each revolution takes T = 1/f = 0.25 s.
questions.explain: Frequency is the number of revolutions completed per unit time, and 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹, one revolution per second. So 4.0 Hz means 4.0 revolutions each second, and each revolution takes T = 1/f = 0.25 s.
questions.working: f = 4.0 Hz = 4.0 s⁻¹: 4.0 revolutions each second. T = 1/f = 1/(4.0 s⁻¹) = 0.25 s per revolution; 4.0 rev/s × 60 s/min = 240 revolutions per minute.

questions.q: An astronaut floats inside a space station that moves in a circular orbit about 400 km above Earth's surface. Which statement about the forces exerted on the astronaut is correct?
options: Earth's gravitational force acts on the astronaut and causes the centripetal acceleration.
No gravitational force acts on the astronaut, as the station is so far from Earth.
Earth's gravitational force is balanced by an outward centrifugal force on it.
Earth's gravitational force acts along with a forward force that keeps it moving.
optionWhy: At 400 km above the surface the astronaut is only about 6% farther from Earth's center than at the surface, so Earth's gravitational force is still large (about 90% of its surface value). It is the force that makes the astronaut, like the station, move in a circle; both fall around Earth together, which is why the astronaut floats.

A student who takes 'weightless' literally picks this. Earth's gravitational force on the astronaut is almost as large as at the surface. Without it the astronaut would move in a straight line, not in a circle around Earth.

A student who believes in a real outward force picks this. No object exerts an outward force on the astronaut. If the forces were balanced, the astronaut would move in a straight line at constant speed; the net force points toward Earth's center.

A student who thinks a moving object needs a forward force picks this. No force along the path is needed to keep the astronaut moving at constant speed; the only force is gravity, perpendicular to the motion, which changes the direction of motion.
questions.explain: At 400 km above the surface the astronaut is only about 6% farther from Earth's center than at the surface, so Earth's gravitational force is still large (about 90% of its surface value). It is the force that makes the astronaut, like the station, move in a circle; both fall around Earth together, which is why the astronaut floats.

questions.q: Two satellites move in circular orbits of the same radius around Earth. Satellite 1 has twice the mass of satellite 2. How does the orbital period of satellite 1 compare with that of satellite 2?
options: It is equal, as the period depends on Earth's mass but not the satellite's.
It is shorter, as Earth pulls harder on the more massive satellite.
It is longer, as the more massive satellite is harder to accelerate.
It cannot be found without knowing the orbital speed of each satellite.
optionWhy: Earth's gravitational force on each satellite, GMm/R², is proportional to the satellite's mass, and so is the force needed for its circular motion, mv²/R. The mass cancels, so T² = (4π²/(GM))R³ depends only on the orbital radius and Earth's mass.

A student who reasons that a heavier object is pulled harder and so moves faster picks this. The pull is larger in proportion to the mass, but so is the force needed to keep the larger mass moving in the circle, so the speed and period are unchanged.

A student who applies 'more mass, less acceleration' picks this, forgetting that the gravitational force is also twice as large. The acceleration GM/R² is the same for both satellites, so their periods are equal.

A student who thinks a satellite can orbit at any speed picks this. At a given radius, gravity must provide exactly v²/R, so the speed, √(GM/R), and the period are fixed by the radius and Earth's mass.
questions.explain: Earth's gravitational force on each satellite, GMm/R², is proportional to the satellite's mass, and so is the force needed for its circular motion, mv²/R. The mass cancels, so T² = (4π²/(GM))R³ depends only on the orbital radius and Earth's mass.

questions.q: A satellite of mass 500 kg moves in a circular orbit around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The only forces are the gravitational forces between the two objects. Which statement correctly compares the gravitational forces that the planet and the satellite exert on each other, and their effects?
options: The planet exerts the larger force, so the satellite has the larger acceleration.
The satellite is too small to exert any gravitational force on the planet.
The forces are equal in magnitude, so the objects have equal accelerations.
The forces are equal in magnitude, and the planet's acceleration is negligible.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the more massive object exerts the larger force picks this. The two forces have equal magnitudes; the satellite accelerates far more because the same force acts on a far smaller mass.
A student who thinks only massive bodies exert gravitational forces picks this. The satellite attracts the planet with a force equal in magnitude to the planet's force on it.
A student who thinks equal forces give equal motions picks this. The forces are equal, but a = F/m: the planet's mass is about 10²² times larger, so its acceleration is negligible.

The forces are a Newton's third-law pair, so they have equal magnitudes. By a = F/m, the planet's acceleration is smaller than the satellite's by the ratio 500 kg/(6.0 × 10²⁴ kg), about 10⁻²², so the planet's motion is negligible.
questions.explain: The forces are a Newton's third-law pair, so they have equal magnitudes. By a = F/m, the planet's acceleration is smaller than the satellite's by the ratio 500 kg/(6.0 × 10²⁴ kg), about 10⁻²², so the planet's motion is negligible.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around a planet. Only the planet's gravitational force is exerted on the satellite, and the planet's motion is negligible. Which quantity changes as the satellite moves around its orbit?
options: The satellite's momentum, since the direction of its velocity changes.
The satellite's angular momentum, since its direction of motion changes.
The system's gravitational potential energy, since the satellite keeps falling.
The satellite's kinetic energy, since the planet's gravity pulls on it.
optionWhy: In a circular orbit the satellite's speed is constant but the direction of its velocity turns continually, so its momentum mv⃗, a vector, changes. Its kinetic energy and angular momentum and the system's U_g and mechanical energy are all constant.

A student who treats angular momentum as momentum by another name picks this. L = rmv sin θ about the planet's center has r, v and θ = 90° all constant in a circular orbit, so L is constant even though the velocity's direction changes.
A student who thinks an orbiting satellite keeps losing U_g because it is falling picks this. U_g = −GMm/r depends only on the separation, which is constant in a circular orbit.

A student who thinks any force on a moving object changes its speed picks this. The gravitational force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, so it does no work and the kinetic energy is constant.
questions.explain: In a circular orbit the satellite's speed is constant but the direction of its velocity turns continually, so its momentum mv⃗, a vector, changes. Its kinetic energy and angular momentum and the system's U_g and mechanical energy are all constant.

questions.q: A probe is launched from the surface of a planet with exactly the escape speed. The planet has no atmosphere, its motion is negligible, and the only force exerted on the probe after launch is the planet's gravitational force. Which statement about the mechanical energy of the probe–planet system is correct?
options: It is zero, and it stays zero at every point of the probe's motion after launch.
It is positive, since the probe needs extra energy to break free of gravity.
It is negative at launch and rises to zero as the probe gets very far away.
It equals the probe's kinetic energy at launch, since U_g is zero at the planet's surface.
optionWhy: Escape speed is defined as the speed that makes the system's mechanical energy zero. Only the internal gravitational force acts, so the mechanical energy stays at that value, zero, throughout the motion.
A student who thinks escape needs positive mechanical energy picks this. Escape speed is the speed that makes K + U_g exactly zero; a positive value would mean a speed greater than the escape speed.
A student who thinks the system gains energy as the probe climbs picks this. With only gravity acting, K + U_g is constant: U_g rises toward zero and K falls by the same amount.

A student who puts the zero of U_g at the planet's surface picks this. For a satellite–planet system U_g is defined to be zero at infinite separation, so at the surface U_g = −GMm/R, which exactly cancels the launch kinetic energy.
questions.explain: Escape speed is defined as the speed that makes the system's mechanical energy zero. Only the internal gravitational force acts, so the mechanical energy stays at that value, zero, throughout the motion.

questions.q: The diagram shows the elliptical orbit of a satellite around a planet whose motion is negligible, with the satellite's distances from the planet's center at its closest point P and its farthest point A, and its speed at P. At P and at A the satellite's velocity is perpendicular to the line from the planet's center. What is the satellite's speed at A?
optionWhy: A student who thinks constant angular momentum means constant speed picks this. L = rmv sin θ includes the distance: at A the satellite is twice as far away, so to keep L constant its speed must be half as large.

The gravitational force points along the line to the planet's center, so it exerts no torque about that point and the satellite's angular momentum is constant. With the velocity perpendicular to the radius at P and A, r_P m v_P = r_A m v_A, so v_A = (8.0 × 10³ m/s)(7.0 × 10⁶ m)/(1.4 × 10⁷ m) = 4.0 × 10³ m/s.

A student who scales the speed with the inverse square of the distance, like the gravitational force, gets (8.0 × 10³ m/s)(1/2)² = 2.0 × 10³ m/s. Angular momentum rmv is constant, so v is inversely proportional to r, not to r², at these two points.

A student who treats the satellite as a point on a rotating object, with v = rω and the same ω, doubles the speed at twice the distance. Nothing keeps the satellite's angular speed constant; its angular momentum is what is constant, so it moves more slowly farther out.
questions.explain: The gravitational force points along the line to the planet's center, so it exerts no torque about that point and the satellite's angular momentum is constant. With the velocity perpendicular to the radius at P and A, r_P m v_P = r_A m v_A, so v_A = (8.0 × 10³ m/s)(7.0 × 10⁶ m)/(1.4 × 10⁷ m) = 4.0 × 10³ m/s.
questions.working: The gravitational force is directed along the line to the planet's center, so it exerts no torque about that point, and the satellite's angular momentum about it is constant. At P and A, sin θ = 1: r_P m v_P = r_A m v_A. v_A = v_P r_P/r_A = (8.0 × 10³ m/s)(7.0 × 10⁶ m)/(1.4 × 10⁷ m) = 4.0 × 10³ m/s.
